faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Sumter walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Sumter lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

Sumter.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Sumter from the historic district, Swan Lake Iris Gardens area, and Shaw-side neighborhoods of the county seat. The homes here sit in a Midlands air-base city ringed by farm and timber land, river swamp, and Carolina bays, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, opossums, gray squirrels, armadillos account for the bulk of our Sumter calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Historic and early-1900s in-town homes, postwar and newer suburbs, and farmhouses on flat sandy lots. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Sumter job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Sumter County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Pinewood home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Start with identification, not panic. Around Pinewood, the everyday snakes are non-venomous rat snakes and racers; the caution species are the copperhead, which is statewide and the venomous snake we encounter most in the Upstate and Midlands. Keep distance, bring pets in, and tell us the size, pattern, and where it sheltered. We identify from photos or on site, handle non-listed snakes where appropriate, and treat venomous encounters as safety work. Reducing cover and rodent food near the foundation lowers repeat sightings more than any single capture.

faqs.q: We found an opossum in our Pinewood crawlspace. What happens next?
faqs.a: In Pinewood, opossums move into crawlspaces through broken vents and loose doors, then rotate dens every few days, which is why sightings come and go. We trap at the access point, remove the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and seal the full foundation line. Securing pet food and trash at night removes the other half of the attraction.

faqs.q: What affects how big a removal job in Pinewood is?
faqs.a: Three things drive a Pinewood job: the species, the structure, and the season. Species decides the method — exclusion for bats, trapping and sealing for raccoons and skunks. Structure decides the labor, since older housing near Pocotaligo swamp and farm country in the county's south often hides several entries behind additions and repairs. Season decides the timing, especially when litters or bat pups mean part of the work waits a few weeks. You get the full picture from the inspection before committing to the plan.

Pinewood.wildlife_intro:
Pinewood keeps our crew busy around the Pocotaligo swamp and farm country in the county's south. Two problems account for most visits: bats behind shutters and in gable vents, and skunks denning under decks.

Postwar brick and frame homes, lake and river cottages, and newer subdivisions share the same streets, with pine canopy hanging over most roofs. Hot summers and mild winters keep Midlands wildlife moving most of the year, and the spring litter season turns small roof gaps into denning calls within weeks.

Removal without repair does not hold in Pinewood, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: An opossum keeps getting under my Mayesville house. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Opossums den under houses because crawlspaces near rail and farm town in the county's east are dry, dark, and close to pet food and trash. One opossum is mostly a nuisance; a season of them brings droppings, torn insulation, and fleas. We trap the animal — opossums are handled under depredation rules, since routine relocation is not permitted in South Carolina — then screen vents and repair the crawlspace door so the shelter is gone, not just the tenant.

faqs.q: How do rats get into Mayesville homes?
faqs.a: Around Mayesville, rats follow food and cover: bird feeders, pet food, ivy and brush against the house, and the lines and limbs that reach the roof near rail and farm town in the county's east. The job is trapping inside, sealing every entry we find, and cutting the routes and food that drew them. We will show you the droppings and rub marks we used to confirm the species, because rat work fails when it is guessed at.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Mayesville home?
faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Mayesville that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Mayesville.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Mayesville and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the rail and farm town in the county's east. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in pine-straw beds and lawns, then about opossums in crawlspaces.

Older homes near the town center give way to ranch subdivisions and then to farmhouses on the outskirts, and the wildlife entries change with each ring. Pine straw is the Midlands detail that matters most: copperheads vanish into it, armadillos root through it, and raccoons cross it nightly from creek woods to rooftops.

Before we leave a Mayesville home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Rembert attic. How is that different from squirrels?
faqs.a: Rats work at night and squirrels work at dawn, which is the first clue. In Rembert, roof rats climb from trees, vines, and utility lines around Wateree-side farm country in the county's northwest, while Norway rats burrow along foundations and come up through plumbing gaps. We identify the species, trap inside the structure, and seal the entry points at roof and foundation level — poison alone leaves dead rats in walls and does nothing about the openings.

faqs.q: How does bat removal work in Rembert?
faqs.a: In Rembert, bat work means exclusion only: one-way devices on the main entries, every other opening sealed, and the colony leaves on its own at dusk. South Carolina does not require a permit for bat removal, and we time full exclusions to SCDNR's guidance windows — early spring or August through October — to avoid trapping flightless young during the summer maternity season. Guano cleanup follows once the attic is empty.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Rembert house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Rembert job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near Wateree-side farm country in the county's northwest with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.

Rembert.wildlife_intro:
The pattern in Rembert is set by the Wateree-side farm country in the county's northwest. If we had to name this town's signature jobs, they would be gray squirrels in mature pine canopy and raccoons working creek corridors.

Brick ranches from the 1960s and 1970s, older in-town homes near the center, and fast-growing subdivisions at the edges give this housing stock three distinct generations of rooflines to inspect. River and lake country surrounds these neighborhoods — creeks, coves, and wooded drains run behind the subdivisions — giving raccoons, squirrels, and bats a covered route to almost every roofline.

Every job in Rembert ends the same way it should: openings found on the inspection closed in steel mesh and flashing, so the house near Wateree-side farm country in the county's northwest stops advertising vacancies to the next animal that passes.
